page: Google Cloud Platform c4d-standard-96 belongs to the General Purpose server family, configured with 96 dedicated vCPUs on the x86_64 architecture and 372.0 GB of system memory. This configuration provides approximately 3.88 GB of RAM per vCPU, maintaining a standard balanced compute-to-memory ratio across large scale virtualized environments.

The instance features dedicated vCPU allocation without integrated hardware accelerators, offering 0 GPUs. It contains no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached storage solutions for operational persistence. Additionally, the instance includes zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, necessitating external networking configurations or proxy gateways for outbound and inbound internet connectivity.

With its high core count and substantial memory capacity, this instance accommodates parallel computing tasks, enterprise web application hosting, continuous integration and continuous deployment pipelines, and intermediate batch data processing. Cost efficiency derives from consolidating compute demands onto a single dedicated node, though the absence of local disks shifts persistence overhead to attached network storage.
description: Google Cloud Platform c4d-standard-96 is a general-purpose instance featuring 96 dedicated vCPUs based on x86_64 architecture and 372.0 GB of system RAM, yielding roughly 3.88 GB of memory per core. The server does not incorporate local storage, meaning disk operations rely entirely on remote storage volumes. Hardware acceleration is absent, as the machine carries zero GPUs. Network architecture provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, which requires network address translation or independent IP allocation for external ingress. Due to its balance of compute and memory at high scale, the configuration fits large multi-threaded application servers, build clusters, CI/CD jobs, ETL pipelines, and horizontally scaled container orchestration platforms. Qualitative cost efficiency is realized through dense resource packaging, balancing compute throughput and memory allocation without auxiliary accelerator hardware overhead.
